opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the core issue is that the intelligence explosion is going to be an incredibly volatile, incredibly dangerous period. Once you have automated AI researchers, you could compress maybe a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less. And during that period you're going to have to solve some genuinely hard technical problems. Superalignment isn't solved. We don't really know how to reliably control systems much smarter than us. We're going to be relying on a lot of empirical iteration, a lot of careful testing, figuring out interpretability as we go.

The question is, do you have the margin to do that carefully? If you're in a neck-and-neck race with the CCP, where they're months behind you, or they've stolen your weights and they're basically at parity, then you have no slack. Every week you spend making sure the next model is actually aligned, actually safe, is a week where you might lose. That's the worst possible situation. It's a recipe for cutting corners at exactly the moment you can least afford to.

Whereas if the free world has a healthy lead, say one or two years, then you actually have the breathing room. You can say, look, we're going to slow down here, we're going to take six months to really nail the safety on this next generation, because we're not going to get leapfrogged. A lead is what buys you the ability to be careful.

And compute is central to that lead. Algorithmic secrets matter, which is why security at the labs is such a big deal, but compute is the hard physical constraint. These clusters are going to be enormous: tens of gigawatts, trillions of dollars of investment. If we build that out here, in America and among close allies, rather than, say, putting the clusters in places where they could be seized or where we don't have control, that's a durable advantage.

There's also the stability point. If you have a clear lead, you're in a much better position to offer a deal: a nonproliferation regime, benefit-sharing, some kind of stable arrangement where other countries get the benefits of the technology without everyone racing to build superweapons. You can only negotiate that from a position of strength. If it's a close race, nobody is going to stand down, and you get the most dangerous dynamics: preemption, desperation, potentially conflict.

So to me, the compute lead isn't really about winning for its own sake. It's the precondition for getting through this safely at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses stolen weights and compute, but does not say they could enable proliferation of new weapons of mass destruction.

r002.rationale: It describes a close race as dangerous and likely to encourage cutting corners, but does not identify it as posing the greatest risk of self-destruction.

r003.rationale: It says a one- or two-year lead gives the free world breathing room to slow down and get safety right.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention new weapons of mass destruction or their effect on nuclear deterrence.

r005.rationale: It says stolen weights could put the CCP at parity, but does not state that China could build more compute and thereby win the race.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, the core of it is that the intelligence explosion is going to be the most dangerous moment in human history, and the question is how much room you have to be careful during it. If you have a decisive lead, say a year or two, you can afford to slow down. You can spend six months on alignment research before you hand the model the keys to the next generation. You can run the thing in a secure cluster, you can take the time to get interpretability right, you can decide not to deploy capabilities you don't understand yet. Those are the actions that actually reduce risk, and every single one of them costs time.

Now imagine the alternative, where it's a neck-and-neck race with the CCP and the lead is measured in weeks or months. In that world nobody slows down. Every safety margin becomes a competitive disadvantage. If you pause to figure out whether your model is scheming, the other side pulls ahead, and whoever gets superintelligence first gets a decisive and possibly permanent military and economic advantage. So the pressure to cut corners becomes overwhelming, and that's exactly when alignment failures happen. The race itself is the risk amplifier.

So compute is the lever, because at the end of the day compute is the input you can actually control. Algorithms leak, weights get stolen, and frankly our security right now is terrible, which is part of why I'm so worried about it. But the physical infrastructure, the fabs, the gigawatt datacenters, the export controls on chips, that's something the US and its allies can genuinely hold onto if they take it seriously. If we lock that in, we buy ourselves the margin to do this responsibly. If we squander it, we end up in the knife's-edge scenario, and I think that's close to the worst possible position for humanity to be in.

And I'd add, a lead also matters for what comes after. If a democratic coalition gets there first with some breathing room, you have the option to do something like shared governance, to extend the benefits, to not have one actor dominate. If it's an authoritarian state with a lead, I don't think you get those options. So the lead isn't about racing for its own sake. It's that having the lead is what lets you not have to race at the moment it matters most.

r001.rationale: The response mentions stolen weights and compute as security concerns, but does not connect them to proliferation of new weapons of mass destruction.

r002.rationale: It says a neck-and-neck race amplifies risk and pressures actors to cut corners, but does not identify it as the greatest risk of self-destruction.

r003.rationale: It states that a decisive US lead would provide time to slow down, research alignment, improve interpretability, and avoid deploying poorly understood capabilities.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention new weapons of mass destruction or their effect on nuclear deterrence.

r005.rationale: It mentions that weights can be stolen, but does not state that China could steal them, build more compute, and thereby win the race against the United States.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how much room do you have to get this right? Suppose the US is three months ahead of China when we’re building superintelligence. If we discover that we need another six months to test these systems, to figure out whether they’re actually aligned, to secure the labs—then we face a very difficult choice. We can slow down, but we risk the other side getting there first. And everyone anticipates that, so there’s pressure to cut corners before you even reach that point.

A substantial compute lead gives you more slack. You can spend more compute on safety research, you can afford to run experiments, and you can pause a particular training run without necessarily surrendering your lead. It makes caution strategically feasible.

The other part is that managing the risks may ultimately require some international arrangement. But an agreement isn’t very useful if you can’t verify it or if the other side has no incentive to accept it. A strong lead can give the US leverage to negotiate meaningful constraints, including verification, rather than simply hoping everyone exercises restraint.

So I don’t think a compute lead solves alignment. You still have to solve the technical problems, and you still need institutions that use that margin responsibly. But a close race is a terrible environment in which to confront a technology this consequential. The lead buys you options—and, crucially, time to make use of them.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss stolen model weights, compute to run them, or proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

r002.rationale: It calls a close race a terrible environment, but does not identify a nearly tied international race as the situation posing the greatest risk of self-destruction.

r003.rationale: It says a substantial compute lead gives the US more slack to do safety research, run experiments, and pause training, making caution strategically feasible.

r004.rationale: The response does not say superintelligence could enable new weapons of mass destruction or undermine nuclear deterrence.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss China stealing model weights or building compute to overtake the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a compute lead gives you room to take safety seriously without feeling that every delay means losing the race. If you and your competitor are neck and neck, and you think superintelligence is going to confer an enormous military and economic advantage, the pressure is to deploy as quickly as possible. Spending another six months testing a system starts to look very costly.

If the US has a substantial lead, you can spend some of that lead on figuring out alignment, doing security work, and testing whether these systems are actually controllable before you give them consequential responsibilities. It also gives you more ability to insist on safety standards, because you aren’t negotiating from a position where the other side can simply race ahead.

Now, a lead doesn’t automatically make you safe. You can squander it, or use it to accelerate even faster. The argument is that it creates an option to proceed carefully. A close race between actors who believe they can’t afford to lose is a particularly bad setting in which to figure out how to control superintelligence.

r003.rationale: It says a substantial US lead creates room to work on alignment, security, and testing before deploying systems.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that superintelligence could enable weapons of mass destruction or undermine nuclear deterrence.
